opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think one of the things I find most exciting in the near term is just how much good advice is locked up in a small number of people's heads, and how unevenly it's distributed.

If you think about it, a lot of what makes some people's lives and careers go well is that they happen to have access to someone wise: a mentor, a well-informed friend, a parent who knows how the system works. Someone who can say, "Here's what you're missing," or "Have you considered this option?" or "I think you're overthinking this, here's what actually matters." Most people don't have that, or they have it for some parts of life and not others. Access to a good doctor who'll actually talk through your situation, a lawyer, someone who understands your finances, someone who can look at your career plan and poke holes in it: that's a pretty elite thing.

What's appealing about AI here is that it could make something like that much more widely available, and pretty soon. Not perfect advice, and I want to be careful there. These systems make mistakes and can be confidently wrong. But the bar to compare against isn't a perfect advisor. It's often nobody, or a random search result, or a friend who means well but doesn't know much. Against that baseline, a patient, knowledgeable system that you can ask follow-up questions, that doesn't get tired of you or judge you for asking something basic, is a pretty big deal.

There's also something I like about the interactivity. A lot of the best advice isn't a fact you look up. It's a back-and-forth where someone helps you figure out what you actually think, what your real constraints are, what you're avoiding. AI is surprisingly good at that kind of thing already, and I think people underrate how valuable it can be to just have something that helps you reason through your own situation.

And then, a little more selfishly from the perspective of someone who thinks about how the world handles the transition to powerful AI: I'm interested in whether AI can help people think more clearly in general. Can it help people reason about evidence, notice when they're being manipulated, and understand complicated issues better? If it can, that's not just good for individuals. It could make society better at making the kinds of high-stakes decisions we're going to face. Of course the flip side is that the same capability could be used to persuade or mislead people, so it really matters how these systems are built and whose interests they're serving. But the upside case is a big part of why I find it exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could make good advice much more widely available soon, including to people who currently lack access to knowledgeable advisers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think one thing that's really interesting about where AI is right now is that a lot of people are focused on the big-picture, transformative stuff — AI doing science, AI automating research, all of that. And I think that's really important. But there's this more mundane thing happening right now, which is that a lot of people have access to a model they can just ask questions, and I think that's actually a pretty big deal in its own right.

The thing I find appealing is that historically, access to good advice has been incredibly unevenly distributed. If you're well-connected, if you have friends who are doctors or lawyers or people who've navigated a particular career, you can just text someone and say, "Hey, is this a big deal? Should I be worried about this? What would you do?" And a huge fraction of people don't have that. They're going through a medical situation or a legal situation or a hard decision about their job, and they're basically on their own, or they're getting whatever comes up on a search engine, which is often pretty bad.

And now you can have something that's kind of like a reasonably knowledgeable friend who has infinite patience, who will engage with the specifics of your situation, who you can ask the embarrassing question to, who you can ask the follow-up question to. It's not perfect — it gets things wrong, and you have to have some judgment about when to trust it. But I think the comparison people make is often to an expert, and the more relevant comparison is to what you actually would have had otherwise, which for a lot of people is nothing, or something much worse.

The other piece I'd point to is that it's just a lot easier to think out loud with something that talks back. A lot of the value of a good advisor isn't that they know some fact you don't — it's that they ask you the question you hadn't asked yourself, or they reflect your reasoning back to you and you notice it doesn't hold up. I've found that AIs can do a surprising amount of that already. And I think over the next few years, that gets dramatically better, and it's kind of a preview of what it looks like when a lot more of the world's knowledge and judgment becomes available to basically anyone who asks.

So I find that pretty exciting, even setting aside all the bigger questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies AI’s current availability to people who can ask it questions as a way to broaden access to good advice, which has historically been unevenly distributed.

astra-6.text:
One thing I find appealing is the possibility of having someone you can talk to at any time, who’s very patient, who knows a lot, and who can help you think through a decision. A lot of the time, when you need advice, you don’t necessarily need some brilliant new insight. You need to lay out what’s going on, have someone ask a few good questions, and look at the situation from a different angle.

And getting that from a person can be hard. They’re busy, or you feel embarrassed asking, or you don’t want to spend an hour giving them all the background. With an AI, you could keep talking until you’ve actually worked through it.

I’d be especially excited about advice that helps you exercise your own judgment: ‘Here are some options you haven’t considered. Here’s an assumption you might want to question.’ Of course, if it just tells you what you want to hear, that could be pretty bad. But the possibility of making a useful thinking partner available to almost anyone seems really appealing.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could make a useful thinking partner available to almost anyone, describing patient, knowledgeable help with decisions as a near-term benefit.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I find appealing is the possibility of everyone having access to a really patient, knowledgeable adviser who’s available whenever they need them. A lot of the time, when you’re trying to make a decision, it helps just to have someone you can talk it through with—someone who will ask questions, help you see options you hadn’t considered, and explain things without making you feel embarrassed for asking.

And access to that kind of help is very uneven right now. Whether you’re thinking about your career or trying to understand some complicated situation, it matters a lot who you know and who has time for you. AI could make that sort of support much more widely available. You’d want to be careful about how much you trust it, but I find that possibility pretty appealing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI could make patient, knowledgeable decision support much more widely available, answering the host’s question about short-run appeal.
